title: The way of not-knowing
hook: Orthodox and mystics say what God is not, since God is beyond every idea

segments.voice: Yesterday, four senses: what happened, what to believe, what to do, and where it leads. Your line was layers of meaning.

The mountain is wrapped in smoke and cloud, and the ground shakes with thunder. The people at the bottom have had enough. They step back and want Moses to speak to them instead of God. Then Exodus gives one quiet sentence: "And the people stood afar off, and Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was." Not into a blaze of light. Into the dark. Some Christians have read that sentence as a map for prayer: the closer you come to God, the less you can see. Today's word: apophatic.

Apophatic is usually explained from a Greek word for saying no. The apophatic way speaks of God by saying what God is not. Not a thing among other things. Not made. Not in one place. Not limited. Not the size of any idea we have. Each not clears away a picture that was too small. Its partner, the cataphatic way, says what God is: good, light, love. Orthodox teaching holds the two together, and gives the not-saying a place of honor; mystics in the West walked the same road. The Bible keeps both in view. God tells Moses, "Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live." A letter to Timothy speaks of God "dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto; whom no man hath seen, nor can see." Light so bright it works like darkness. Gregory of Nyssa, writing about the life of Moses, noticed the order of the story: Moses meets God first in light, at the burning bush, later in cloud, and at last in thick darkness. For Gregory, going deeper meant seeing less, and knowing more. In medieval England, an unknown writer made a small book of it, The Cloud of Unknowing. Its counsel, put simply: you won't reach God by thinking harder; reach into the cloud with love. None of this is the same as knowing nothing. It keeps God larger than your best idea, and lets silence say what words can't.

Whatever you believe, try this as an exercise: on each out-breath, set down one picture of God that's too small. Not an old man on a cloud, not a vending machine, not my worst fear, not my best idea either. When you run out, sit in the space that's left without filling it; if you pray, let that empty space be your prayer.
Apophatic. The way of not-knowing: speaking of God by saying what God is not, because God is beyond every idea.
Your line: more than you think. Silence can say it too. Day one thousand sixty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Orthodox Christians speak of God both by what God is and, with special honor, by what God is not; in the West, contemplative Christians practice a similar wordless prayer, drawing on books like The Cloud of Unknowing.

fork.reveal: "Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was." Gregory of Nyssa read it as the deepest stage: going further in meant seeing less.

chat.says: Isn't saying what God is not just a fancy way of saying you know nothing?
options: No. Each not clears away a picture too small for God, keeping God larger than our ideas.
Yes. It means Christians shouldn't call God good or loving, only say what God isn't.
It's a Western idea from medieval England that the Orthodox churches never use.
chat.meaning: The apophatic way isn't knowing nothing. Each not clears away a picture that was too small, and it sits alongside saying what God is.
